value.overview: The Upland Sandpiper is a long-legged, long-winged shorebird that spends most of its time on dry ground rather than in wetlands. It breeds mainly in grasslands of North America and migrates to open country in South America. Its slender neck, small dove-like head, large dark eye, and thin bill give it an unusual appearance among sandpipers. It is also known for a distinctive mellow whistle and for perching on fence posts and other elevated structures.
value.classification: The Upland Sandpiper belongs to the sandpiper family, Scolopacidae, in the order Charadriiformes. It is the only living species in the genus Bartramia.
value.identification: This medium-sized shorebird measures about 28–32 cm long and has a wingspan near 47 cm. Adults are mottled golden-brown and dark above, with whitish underparts marked by dark streaks and chevrons on the breast and sides. It has long legs, a long tail, a thin straight bill, a white throat, and a pale eyering. In flight, a narrow white area on the outer wing may be visible. Its upright posture and terrestrial habits are distinctive.
value.rangeHabitat: The Upland Sandpiper breeds from southern Canada through much of the central United States, especially in native prairie and other open grasslands. It also uses pastures, fallow fields, hayfields, airfields, and lightly vegetated agricultural areas. It winters mainly in the pampas and llanos of South America. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon to rare nonbreeding migrant and does not breed. Individuals may occur in open grasslands, pastures, agricultural fields, airfields, and other short-grass habitats, including sites along both slopes and the Pacific lowlands.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant, it moves south from North America after breeding and returns north in spring. In Costa Rica it is primarily a passage migrant or occasional nonbreeding visitor, with records concentrated during migration rather than representing a resident population. It is generally uncommon and may be overlooked because it favors dry, open fields instead of muddy shorelines.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in open grasslands with short to moderately tall vegetation and little woody cover. The nest is a shallow depression on the ground, usually concealed among grasses. The clutch commonly contains four eggs, and both adults may participate in incubation and care of the young. Males perform conspicuous song flights and often call while perched on fence posts or other elevated objects. After hatching, adults and chicks forage together in open country.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, including grasshoppers, crickets, beetles, caterpillars, ants, spiders, earthworms, snails, and millipedes. Seeds of grasses, weeds, and other plants are also eaten. The bird usually feeds by walking briskly through short vegetation and picking prey from the ground or low plants. Migrants may forage in pastures, fallow fields, recently burned areas, and other open habitats where insects are abundant.
value.behavior: The Upland Sandpiper is an unusually terrestrial shorebird and is rarely associated with beaches or shallow water. It often walks steadily through grassland, pauses to look around, and raises its wings briefly after landing. During the breeding season, males give a distinctive mellow, whistled song from fence posts, utility poles, or the air. Song flights involve graceful circling and fluttering high above the territory. Migration commonly occurs at night, often in loose groups that call to one another.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered broadly stable, although declines have occurred in parts of eastern North America and some regional populations remain under pressure. The global breeding population has been estimated at roughly 750,000 individuals.
